messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Precompiled header confusion
parts:
I just wanted to address a point about precompiled headers while it's still in my memory.


On Sat, Apr 13, 2013 at 5:57 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
I was getting ready to run this tool again. But first I ran into an issue that confused me. I had thought that

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ find src/stan -name '*.hpp' -print | xargs -n 1 -P 7 clang++ -x c++-header -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2/ -I lib/boost_1.53.0/ -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS 2> /tmp/pch_errors.txt

would succeed in making a precompiled header out of every .hpp file in stan/src/.

I also had the same misconception about precompiled headers. For any build, there can only be 1 (one) precompiled header. It has to be included first in the file and it only works under certain compilers. (I think it doesn't work for Windows g++ and Mac's clang++, but it does work for Mac g++.) I've made that mistake and built one for each header (which took hours) only to find out that's not how it works.

For our build, that single header is src/stan/model/model_header.hpp. That's why it has so much included int it. If after a build, you see a src/stan/model/model_header.hpp.pch or model_header.hpp.gch, you've got a precompiled header. The flags that control it in our build are in os_* and the variable is called PCH. The place it actually gets built is in make/models towards the end.

I haven't successfully gotten the build time down by using a precompiled header. The issue we have is the number of template instantiations going on, which can't be addressed with the precompiled header. What Bob's suggested in his 3/20 email titled "how much can we precompile? + privacy" is where we could actually make improvements to our build times. This is the section that's relevant:


On Wed, Mar 20, 2013 at 2:57 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
Topic I
-------

One issue that would be nice to address in this
refactoring is the time it takes to compile user models.

One thing we could do to speed this up is more
agressively precompile our libs.

The most general way to do this is to follow the
pattern set up in the grammars (which was forced
upon us by Windows compiler lameness).

The general idea is for each function foo()
would be to have three separate files:

   foo.hpp   pure header file, included by clients
             who link against the precompile lib

   foo_def.hpp   actual definitions, included by
                 clients who want to use Stan as
                 a header only lib

   foo_inst.cpp  instantiations of the function's templates,
                 compiled into an archive for users to link
                 against;  includes foo_def.hpp

Right now, the boundary between what gets separated
into .hpp and .cpp files seems rather arbitrary.





At this point, I'm all for splitting our build. I think we can engineer it so that it costs a bunch of time once to build out the instantiations that would be standard in a Stan build, and then every model would be relatively quick to compile. It would cost us some time to engineer it properly, but we can eat that cost. (By we, I mean I'm willing to volunteer if no one else steps up.)


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Precompiled header confusion
parts:
On Sunday, April 14, 2013 11:55:15 PM UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
I just wanted to address a point about precompiled headers while it's still in my memory.
On Sat, Apr 13, 2013 at 5:57 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
I was getting ready to run this tool again. But first I ran into an issue that confused me. I had thought that

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ find src/stan -name '*.hpp' -print | xargs -n 1 -P 7 clang++ -x c++-header -I src -I lib/eigen_3.1.2/ -I lib/boost_1.53.0/ -Wall -DBOOST_RESULT_OF_USE_TR1 -DBOOST_NO_DECLTYPE -DBOOST_DISABLE_ASSERTS 2> /tmp/pch_errors.txt

would succeed in making a precompiled header out of every .hpp file in stan/src/.

I also had the same misconception about precompiled headers. For any build, there can only be 1 (one) precompiled header. It has to be included first in the file and it only works under certain compilers. (I think it doesn't work for Windows g++ and Mac's clang++, but it does work for Mac g++.) I've made that mistake and built one for each header (which took hours) only to find out that's not how it works.

Right, I can see why if you wanted to use a precompiled header to (possibly) speed up the build time, you would want a single .pch file rather than one .pch file per .hpp file. But as a matter of testing whether your .hpp files are valid, it seems that testing whether the .hpp file can be made into a .pch file successfully is a potentially valid test. I had thought that it would be the same as gtesting

#include <foo.hpp>
#include <gtest/gtest.h>

TEST(foo,headerParses) {
  EXPECT_TRUE(true);
}

but apparently gtesting that is not as extensive as precompiling foo.hpp into foo.pch.

Ben
